title: Couples Tied Together on an Obstacle Course
text:
Many long relationships slip from early excitement into comfortable routine. Arthur Aron and his colleagues proposed that couples could recover some of the early spark by doing new and challenging things together, so that the excitement of the activity became linked with the partner.

After surveys suggested that couples who shared exciting activities were happier, the researchers tested the idea in the laboratory at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. Married couples first filled out questionnaires about their relationship. Then some couples were given a novel and mildly arousing task. Their wrists and ankles were bound together with Velcro straps, and they had to crawl on gym mats across the room and over a barrier, pushing a foam cylinder without using their hands or teeth, then turn around and come back, all against a time limit with a prize at stake. Other couples did a dull version: one partner slowly rolled a ball to the middle of the room while the other watched.

Afterward the couples again rated their relationship. Those who had stumbled, laughed and struggled through the obstacle course together reported a greater increase in relationship quality than those who had done the mundane task. Later experiments by the team found similar results.
lesson: Break routine together. Trying something new and a little challenging as a couple, or as a family, can renew a bond that has gone flat.
people: Arthur Aron, Christina Norman, Elaine Aron, Colin McKenna, Richard Heyman
location: State University of New York at Stony Brook, Stony Brook, USA
source: Aron, A., Norman, C. C., Aron, E. N., McKenna, C., and Heyman, R. E. (2000). Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273-284.
